newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-N Flinders may spend A$40m on Callie.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-N Flinders may spend A$40m on Callie.

text.p: North Flinders Mines Ltd may have to spend up to A$40 million on a hoisting shaft for the planned underground mine at Callie in the Northern Territory, executive chairman Tony Palmer said on Thursday.

Palmer told reporters after the company's annual meeting the Callie Wilson Shoot resource was now confirmed by drilling to extend to 550 metres below surface and further studies on underground development currently were underway.
"There is no doubt (a shaft) is necessary, the question is when," he said, adding that depending on depth and tonnages, it was not uncommon for shaft facilities to cost A$40 million.
Palmer earlier told shareholders grades from sampling in the upper part of Wilson Shoot were generally consistent with average predicted grades but variable as expected.
A trial processing of underground ore would be completed early in the December quarter of 1996/97, he said.

Palmer warned unit costs would rise when production based at Callie moved underground, to be offset to some extent by higher average mined grades, and said the ongoing capital demands of an underground development would require vigilant planning.

Following a series of shareholder questions about the North Flinders takeover bid by Normandy Mining Ltd, Palmer told reporters key stakeholder, French fund manager Societe Generale, had made it clear it was not going to accept the offer.
"I suppose when you say how confident am I that they will (accept), I am pretty confident they probably won't is the answer," he said.
However, Palmer, who is also Normandy's managing director, said Normandy had not conceded defeat at all.

"If we continue to get dribs and drabs and we meet the three quarters of shareholders (accepting) criteria then ... you have only got to convince (Societe Generale fund manager) Guy Borel and you are there," he said.
Palmer earlier told shareholders Normandy on Wednesday had increased its stake in North Flinders to 73.7 percent, with acceptances from 55 percent of shareholders.
With the bid extended until November 4, Palmer said he did not know how many more extensions there may be.

Asked if North Flinders was seeking prospects outside the Tanami desert region, Palmer said the company's cash balance was not so healthy because of the demands of Callie and it was felt wise to focus on the Tanami where there was so much potential to be unlocked.
However, he said the company had not "ruled the page off altogether" and always considered any offer.
